title: The gates of tears (Berakhot 32b)
hookLine: since the Temple fell the gates of prayer may be locked, but the gates of tears are never locked
tomorrow: a snake bites him in the middle of prayer. why doesn't he stop?

cards: Some people can't cry at the sad part of a movie, then cry at a commercial a week later. Tears keep their own schedule.
Rabbi Elazar says something hard: since the day the Temple was destroyed, the gates of prayer have been locked. So what's left? He finishes the thought.
Even though the gates of prayer are locked, the gates of tears are not.

teach.h: LAMENTATIONS: HE SHUTS OUT MY PRAYER.
teach.b: He brings a verse for each gate. For the locked one, Lamentations: "Also when I cry and shout, he shutteth out my prayer."

teach.h: THE PSALM: HOLD NOT THY PEACE AT MY TEARS.
teach.b: For the open one, a psalm: "Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears." Words can feel like they're hitting a closed door. Tears, Rabbi Elazar says, still get through.
Now look at where this lands, at the end of the week. Yochanan ben Zakkai wept and said, I don't know. Set words needed something new each time.
The early pious prepared their hearts before a word was said. Hannah whispered, then made a bold case. Moses grabbed hold and pleaded for others.

teach.h: THE WEEK, WHEN WORDS RUN OUT.
teach.b: Tears are where all of that goes when the words run out. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight.
In this teaching, crying isn't a failure to pray.
It may be the prayer that still gets in.

how: Jewish prayer has long made room for tears, from the psalms to the High Holy Day services, and Rabbi Elazar's saying about the gates of tears is often quoted to comfort people who find it hard to pray in words.

games.q: what does “the gates of tears” mean?
o: a gate in Jerusalem where mourners once gathered
a season of the year set aside for public mourning
tears reach God even when words feel shut out

p: hold not thy peace at my tears

s: crying while you pray means the prayer failed
Rabbi Elazar: the gates of tears are not locked.
Rabbi Elazar says the gates of prayer have been locked since the Temple was destroyed
and even so, the gates of tears are open.

games.q: your friend apologizes for crying during a memorial service. what does Berakhot 32b let you say?
o: no need to apologize: the gates of tears are never locked.
crying is fine, but it doesn't count as part of the prayer.
wait until you're calm, and then you can pray properly.
games.why: Rabbi Elazar: even when the gates of prayer are locked, the gates of tears are open, and he brings a psalm to show it.

practice: Sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up. Let whatever is close to the surface come up, without pushing it down or forcing it. If something wells up, let it; if nothing does, the open hands are enough.

wordCard.voice: The gates of tears. Rabbi Elazar: the gates of prayer may be locked, but the gates of tears are not.

orig.note: Hebrew: the gates of tears, which Rabbi Elazar says are never locked.

carryVoice: Your line: the gates of tears. Words can stall, and tears still get in. Twenty-five of fifty, halfway through Berakhot.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 32b (Rabbi Elazar: the gates of prayer locked since the Temple was destroyed; the gates of tears not locked)
